pr_body:
# Objective

- Add basic exposure settings for aperture in f-stops, shutter speed in seconds, and sensitivity in ISO units as per Google's Filament: https://google.github.io/filament/Filament.html#physicallybasedcamera
- Fixes #8369 

## Solution

- Add basic exposure settings for aperture in f-stops, shutter speed in seconds, and sensitivity in ISO units as per Google's Filament: https://google.github.io/filament/Filament.html#physicallybasedcamera

---

## Changelog

- Added: ExposureSettings component that can be added to an entity with a Camera to configure PBR exposure settings

## Migration Guide

- The `ExposureSettings` component on an `Camera` entity will be used to configure exposure for PBR rendering. Previously only directional lights were using hard-coded exposure, but now all light has exposure applied. This will mean that all light sources other than directional lights will be significantly darker. Adjust the exposure settings and light intensities as necessary.

I'd suggest against changing the default intensities for point/spot lights. An 800 lumen (i.e., 60 W incandescent brightness) light is more likely to be what a user wants compared to a 3.6 million lumen one. It means that, say, a flashlight will be completely overpowered by the light of the sun, but that's true in the real world too!

Rather, the main suggested mitigation should be to specify exposure settings corresponding to an indoor or night scene. Then making sure the scale of the scene is accurate in meters. And only once those are both calibrated should you start increasing the number/brightness of lights.

I did some investigation of Blender's handling of light intensity and I'm somewhat skeptical that their brightness levels are even meaningful...

Apparently, Blender uses a [hard-coded conversion factor](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF-Blender-IO/blob/356b3dda976303d3ecce8b3bd1591245e576db38/addons/io_scene_gltf2/blender/com/gltf2_blender_conversion.py#L19) of 683 lumens/watt when exporting gltf (applied [here](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF-Blender-IO/blob/356b3dda976303d3ecce8b3bd1591245e576db38/addons/io_scene_gltf2/blender/exp/gltf2_blender_gather_lights.py#L95)). While the Blender documentation provides a [table of common wattage values](https://docs.blender.org/manual/en/latest/render/lights/light_object.html#power-of-lights) with conversion ratio varying from 227 lumens/watt to 556 lumens/watt.

The term for this conversion factor seems to be [luminous efficacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminous_efficacy). And from what I can find online, the 683 lumens/watt number seems to be a theoretical upper bound and values as low as 15 lumens/watt apply to some light sources.

Weirdly, I wasn't able to find any reference to how Blender determines how much of a light source's power is visible light. That feels like a rather relevant factor given that the whole reason there isn't only one luminous efficacy value is because different kinds of light have differently shaped spectrums

If I change the default exposure from `EV100_OVERCAST: f32 = 12.0` to `EV100_INDOOR: f32 = 7.0` everything does start to line up roughly with what I see in Blender. If their brightness levels aren't meaningful to reason about I think it's a good enough approximation.

Having a default exposure of 7 instead of 12 also avoids having intensity/illuminance values in the 10000s in the examples.

Here are some comparisons with an exposure of 7, with the Blender exposure and other settings at the default:
Point light 10W (Blender default).
![Screenshot 2023-12-16 115422](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/assets/23659539/0ec25ec7-3244-4de0-8ca0-47239a9cc4f3)

Directional light 1W/m^2 (also Blender default. I assume they use 1W/m^2 as a default because the default exposure is for indoor scenes, and 1000W/m^2 (strength of the sun according to the Blender docs) would blow out the scene).
![Screenshot 2023-12-16 115700](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/assets/23659539/7d5143ab-f1ea-42b4-b4c8-8cff414c3f56)

issue_context.title: EnvironmentMap modulation
issue_context.body:
## What problem does this solve or what need does it fill?

I'd like to be able to simulate day / night cycles in my game. Unfortunately this is hard to do when using environment maps because the intensity of the map is fixed, so the daytime sky is at full brightness even in the middle of the night.

## What solution would you like?

I'd like to be able to set a modulation intensity for an environment map. Note that three.js has this feature (but only on a per-material basis - I want it to be global).

Ideally, I would use two environment maps, one representing the daytime sky and one representing the nighttime. At noon, the intensity of the daytime env map would be one, and the intensity of the night time map would be 0. The opposite would be true at midnight. The intensity of each map would be interpolated based on the diurnal cycle.

Alternatively, if it is only possible to have a single env map, then I would just have one map for the daytime, and no map for the nighttime.

## What alternative(s) have you considered?

Well, one solution is to use ambient light (which can be modulated) instead of environment maps, but you lose a lot in scene quality especially for reflective materials. Alternatively, one could have a whole bunch of environment maps and switch between them, but this would consume a lot of memory.

## Additional context

There's been a discussion on the three.js issue tracker about adding global backround intensity for environment maps. Although the idea is generally favorable, the discussion is stalled because of concerns about backwards incompatibility with the existing per-material intensity setting. Since Bevy doesn't have this feature, backwards compatibility is not a concern.
comments: Seems like a sensible request: feel free to make a PR!

I'm in favor of adding this. The only part that needs discussion is how are we going to specify the "strength"?

DirectionalLights use lux, and Point/Spot Lights use lumens (although the docs suck, that's a different issue). 

We could specify the EnvironmentMapLight as a simple multiplier, or in one of these units, or as an Ev100 exposure, or something else.

The recent God of War: Ragnarok presentation has some info on how they manage physical lighting values https://sms.playstation.com/media/documents/GOWR_Stephen_Mcauley_RenderingGOWR_GDC23.pdf.

CC @superdump
The main constraint is that the default value should preserve the existing behavior. Other than that I don't care.
